n: The heading calls this ‘A prayer of the afflicted, when he is overwhelmed.’ It begins with a simple plea that God would truly hear.

f.w: let my cry come unto thee

n: He begs God not to turn away in his time of trouble but to listen closely and answer quickly.
His days vanish like smoke, and his body burns as if with fever, like coals in a fireplace.
His heart is struck and dried up like sun-scorched grass, so that he loses all appetite. Grief can affect the whole body.
Groaning and grief have left him so thin that his skin clings to his bones.
He compares himself to lonely birds of desolate places, symbols of isolation. The exact species are uncertain.

f.g: A bird of uncertain kind living in ruins or desert — possibly a jackdaw or owl.
Owls were associated with ruins and loneliness.

n: He lies awake like a solitary bird on a flat rooftop — sleepless and alone.
Enemies taunt him constantly, and those who rage against him use his name as a curse.

f.g: They use my name in their curses.

n: Ashes, a sign of mourning, are like his daily bread, and his tears mix into his drink.
He feels God lifted him up only to throw him down, like a wind lifting and dropping a leaf.

f.w: lifted me up, and cast me down

n: His life is like a lengthening evening shadow that will soon disappear, and he withers like grass.
The turning point: ‘But thou, O LORD.’ Though he fades, God endures forever and is remembered in every generation.
He looks beyond his own pain to Zion’s future. God will rise and have compassion on her, for the appointed time has come. This may reflect hopes for rebuilding Jerusalem after the exile.
God’s servants love even Zion’s ruined stones and dust. Their love for the city mirrors God’s own.
Zion’s restoration will lead the nations and their kings to revere the Lord.

f.w: all the kings of the earth

n: When the Lord builds Zion, he will appear in glory. Latter-day Saints see this as a prophecy of the latter-day building of Zion before Christ’s return.
God pays attention to the prayers of the destitute — those stripped of everything — and never scorns them.
This hope is written down so future generations — people not yet born — will praise the Lord too.

f.w: written for the generation to come

n: God looks down from his heavenly sanctuary to see the earth.

f.w: looked down from the height of his sanctuary

n: He hears the groans of prisoners and frees those condemned to die — an image Latter-day Saints also connect with Christ’s work among the dead.

f.g: Literally ‘sons of death,’ those condemned to die.

n: Those he frees will proclaim the Lord’s name in Zion and Jerusalem.
Nations and kingdoms will gather together to serve the Lord.

f.w: the kingdoms, to serve the LORD

n: Back to his own situation: in the middle of his life’s journey, God has drained his strength and cut his days short.

f.g: Along the road of life; midway.

n: He pleads not to be taken in the middle of his life — contrasting his few years with God’s endless ones.

f.w: in the midst of my days

n: God laid the earth’s foundations long ago and made the heavens. Hebrews applies verses 25–27 to Jesus Christ as Creator.

f.w: laid the foundation of the earth

n: Even heaven and earth will wear out like old clothes, and God will change them like a garment. Scripture teaches the earth will be renewed and glorified.
But God never changes, and his years will never end. This constancy is the anchor of hope.
Because God endures, so will his people’s descendants. The psalmist’s personal hope widens into hope for the generations to come.

f.w: The children of thy servants shall continue
